newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS--up as tightening fears ease.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS--up as tightening fears ease.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds rose two to three basis points, with discount bonds getting the biggest mark-ups, as the latest comments from the Federal Reserve chairman sparked doubts a tightening might be imminent.

But traders noted that there were differing opinions over how to interpret the latest speech by Alan Greenspan, the head of the central bank, with some saying the prospect that interest rates would be raised on May 20, when the Fed's policy-making arm next meets, remained a strong possibility.
"A lot of people are wandering around and trying to figure out why the market is up. I guess it depends on what headline you read."

Despite New York City's prediction that it not only will end the 1997 fiscal year on June 30 with an estimated $856 million surplus, but follow it up with a projected $200 million surplus next year, traders said the city's debt did not outpace the rest of the market.
"They're just kind of trading the way they have. The one thing they have going against them is that a lot of portfolio managers are pretty well loaded up on cities," a trader said.

He noted that such big institutional players typically need to diversify their holdings, which limits how much they can buy of one issuer, even though New York City is one of the biggest names in the market, and its paper one of the most liquid.

The slightly bigger rise seen in discount bonds showed that at least some market participants look for the market's recent rises to continue, as current coupon paper lagged. They pointed to part of Greenspan's speech that supported views that a near-term tightening no longer was as likely.
The nation's dominant setter of monetary policy said that while he expected growth to slow later this year and into next, the Federal Reserve was prepared to act if that does not prove to the case.

According to a text of his speech, Greenspan said: "Should the expected slowing in the growth of demand fail to materialize, we would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets."
"It seems to me that the people buying don't necessarily want to buy, it's because they're short futures," a trader said.
He added: "I personally want to sell, I don't see a tremendous upside," he said, explaining he believed the Federal Reserve Chairman had signaled another interest rate hike likely would be needed.
In debt futures, June U.S. Treasury bonds gained 11 ticks to 110-5/32, while June municipal bonds climbed nine ticks to 115-18/32. This left the MOB spread at plus 173 ticks.

A key gauge of the secondary market, the Standard and Poor's Blue List, climbed to $1.019 billion, suggesting supplies are fattening. The measure had fallen to $800 million to $900 million earlier this week.
However, preliminary soundings of the market suggested the supply of new municipal bonds might fall to as low as $1.8 billion next week, down sharply from about $3.8 billion this week.
In the seondary market, Chicago, Illinois Board of Education Chicago School Reform of December 2020, which pay a 5-3/4 percent coupon, were bid at 5.86 percent, NET, down three basis points.
Port Seattle Washington Revenues of October 2027, which carry a 5-1/2 percent coupon, were bid at 5.75 percent, NET, down two basis points.
